result: 83 long COVID patients with neurological symptoms had lower global cognition than 22 infection-recovered controls (ACE-III OCLz -0.39 vs +0.32, P<0.01), 48% had episodic memory deficits, and patients had thinner left posterior superior temporal cortex and lower FA/higher RD in widespread white matter that correlated with cognitive deficits.
reason: Long COVID version of the cognitive deficit finding, not an independent ME/CFS replication; small control group, screening test

result: Of 112 of 460 contacted patients discharged from a UK long COVID service (mean 37.6 months post-infection), 90.2% still had symptoms and disability, mean EQ-5D-5L index was 0.53, and 43% met suspected NICE ME/CFS criteria.
reason: Adds a longer (about 3-year) persistence time course; low response rate (24%) and self-report criteria, not an incidence replication

result: Of 112 of 460 contacted patients discharged from a UK long COVID service, 90.2% still had symptoms and 43% met suspected NICE ME/CFS criteria.

result: In 12 post-COVID ME/CFS patients, immunoadsorption nearly eliminated ANSR autoantibodies and lowered cytokines and soluble spike, improved neuropsychological function and handgrip at 30 days, but did not improve self-reported symptoms or ME/CFS scores, and the removed proteins rebounded within a month.
reason: already cited (preprint of Anft 2025, Mol Ther; identical 12-patient study and results)

result: In 12 post-COVID ME/CFS patients, open-label immunoadsorption removed ANSR autoantibodies and lowered cytokines, improved neuropsychological tests and handgrip at 30 days, but self-reported symptoms and ME/CFS questionnaire scores did not improve and antibodies rebounded within a month.
reason: Uncontrolled 12-patient series (preprint of Anft 2025); consistent with the null controlled trials and adds rebound/mechanism data, not a replication of a controlled trial

result: Meta-analysis of 37 studies (543 ME/CFS, 651 FM vs 747 and 447 controls) found elevated baseline adrenaline in ME/CFS (SMD 0.49, 95% CI 0.31-0.67) and atypical adrenergic responses to exercise, with adrenergic dysfunction mainly in ME/CFS rather than fibromyalgia.
reason: Plasma adrenaline is covered by the newer neuro-plasma-adrenaline finding; pooled meta-analysis adds an FM comparison and exercise responses (check whether already cited there)

result: In 376 long COVID participants rating 8 symptoms every 3 h for up to 24 days, all symptoms rose within 30 min of physical, cognitive and social activity (fatigue +1.8/10 after highest physical exertion, +1.5 after cognitive effort), with only mild delayed fatigue at 3 h (0.3) or one day (0.2).
reason: Tests symptom timing after exertion and finds mainly immediate rather than delayed worsening; long COVID sample not selected for PEM and everyday rather than standardised exertion

result: In 376 long COVID participants with 3-hourly ecological momentary assessment, symptoms rose within 30 min of all activity types in proportion to effort (fatigue +1.8/10 after highest physical exertion), with only mild delayed fatigue at 3 h or one day.
reason: Symptom-tracking study of post-exertional worsening in long COVID; adds dose-response, immediate timing and cognitive/social triggers (also relevant to neuro-nonphysical-triggers)

result: In a stratified random sample of 9,825 KPNC adults (population 2.7 million), 1.67% (95% CI 1.20-2.15%) had self-reported ME/CFS-like illness meeting IOM symptom criteria, and 14.12% of these cases arose after COVID-19, with no substantial pandemic-related rise.
reason: Independent US population prevalence estimate by self-reported IOM symptoms, at the upper end like NHIS; adds the post-COVID share; sex split not in abstract

result: Among 88 Charité post-COVID follow-up patients, the fatigue/exertional-intolerance group (n=36) had lower respiratory muscle strength (median 55.8% vs 70.6% and 76.8% predicted, p=0.011) and more complex ventilatory dysfunction (reduced FVC with normal TLC; 88.9% vs 29.1% and 25.0%).
reason: No CPET or peak VO2 measured; respiratory muscle weakness suggests neuromuscular involvement in fatigue-type long COVID, a loose fit to the long COVID myopathy finding
